reference.source: Vascular surgery and sports medicine references
clinicalPearls: An uncommon cause of exertional calf pain in young, often athletic, individuals due to compression of the popliteal artery
It should be considered when a fit young person has claudication without atherosclerotic risk factors
Symptoms are provoked by exercise, particularly activities using the calf muscles, and relieved by rest
Compression usually results from an abnormal anatomical relationship between the artery and the gastrocnemius or popliteus, though a functional form exists
Provocative manoeuvres with active plantarflexion can reproduce reduced pedal pulses and imaging changes
Untreated repetitive compression can damage the artery, causing stenosis, thrombosis or aneurysm, so surgery is often required
reference.pathophysiology: Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome arises when the popliteal artery is compressed within the popliteal fossa, most often by an anomalous course relative to the medial head of gastrocnemius or by an accessory muscle slip; a functional variant occurs with a hypertrophied but normally positioned muscle. Repetitive compression during exercise transiently reduces distal flow, causing claudication, and over time causes intimal injury that can progress to fixed stenosis, thrombosis or post-stenotic aneurysm with distal embolisation. The young age and absence of atherosclerotic risk factors distinguish it from typical peripheral arterial disease.
additionalDifferentials: Cystic adventitial disease of the popliteal artery
Nerve entrapment causing exertional leg pain
additionalInvestigations: Ankle-brachial index and pulse assessment at rest and with provocation
Duplex ultrasound with active plantarflexion manoeuvres
CT or MR angiography, including provocative positioning, to show compression and anatomy
Assessment for arterial damage such as stenosis, thrombosis or aneurysm
redFlags: Signs of arterial thrombosis or acute limb ischaemia
Distal embolisation or a popliteal aneurysm
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis and surgical release, and vascular reconstruction if the artery is damaged, outcomes are generally good; delayed diagnosis risks permanent arterial injury and limb-threatening complications.
pitfalls: Dismissing exertional leg pain in a young athlete as musculoskeletal
Confusing it with chronic exertional compartment syndrome
Relying on resting vascular studies, which may be normal without provocation
Missing established arterial damage requiring reconstruction
management: Operative decompression by dividing the compressing gastrocnemius or popliteus muscle slip or correcting the anomalous arterial course, the mainstay of treatment
Vascular reconstruction with vein bypass or interposition graft where recurrent compression has caused fixed stenosis, thrombosis or aneurysm
Temporary avoidance of triggering calf-loading exercise until surgical release
Thrombolysis or thrombectomy with antiplatelet cover for acute arterial thrombosis
Evaluation of the opposite leg because the anomaly is often bilateral
Referral to vascular surgery and sports medicine for timely diagnosis and rehabilitation after repair
